facts.fact: The Museum Angewandte Kunst is a museum of applied art on Frankfurt's Museumsufer (Museum Riverbank).
facts.quote: The Museum Angewandte Kunst (MAK) is located in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, and is part of Frankfurt's Museumsufer (Museum Riverbank).

facts.fact: Richard Meier designed the building, folding the 19th-century Neoclassicist Metzler villa into an ensemble of park, villa and new building.
facts.quote: The architecture housing the Museum Angewandte Kunst was designed by Richard Meier. By integrating the Neoclassicist Metzler family villa built in the nineteenth century, he created an ensemble consisting of the surrounding park, the villa, and the new building.

facts.fact: The building recalls Le Corbusier's houses, drawing on Classical Modern architecture's plain forms and clearly articulated volumes.
facts.quote: The Museum Angewandte Kunst building evokes Le Corbusier's residential houses. For stylistic orientation, the architect Richard Meier looks to Classical Modern architecture with its straightforward forms and clearly articulated spatial bodies.

facts.fact: Meier used the old villa as a module for the whole design; the new building was completed in 1987.
facts.quote: When it came time to expand the museum's facilities, the villa served the American architect Richard Meier as a module in the design of the overall concept for the new construction. The latter, completed in 1987, is thus a modern response to the existing structure, in which Meier transformed the ground plan and residential character into an independent museum architecture.

facts.fact: A 2013 refit removed partitions and additions from the 1990s, bringing back Meier's light-filled, interlocking spaces with views of the park and river.
facts.quote: Since the spring of 2013, following a structural alteration phase in which older partitions and structural additions of the 1990s were removed, visitors have once again had the opportunity to experience the original Richard Meier architecture: light-flooded spaces, interlocking generously and granting a view of the park and river.

facts.fact: The villa it builds on is a three-storey house on a square plan with five window bays on each side, built in 1804.
facts.quote: The present-day Historic Villa Metzler was built in 1804 for the apothecary Peter Salzwedel as a summer house located on the outskirts of the town. On a square ground plan, a structure rises up three storeys, exhibiting five window axes on each side and a classical sense of balance.

facts.fact: The museum's park links it to the Museum der Weltkulturen and gives the Sachsenhausen district a way through to the river Main.
facts.quote: The museum park connects the Museum Angewandte Kunst with the Museum der Weltkulturen, while also serving as a "passageway" to the Main for the residents of the Sachsenhausen district.

facts.fact: Munkegaard School is a school in Gentofte, north of Copenhagen, designed by Arne Jacobsen and completed in 1957.
facts.quote: Munkegaard School (Danish: Munkegårdsskolen) is a school in Gentofte, just north of Copenhagen, designed by the Danish architect Arne Jacobsen and completed in 1957.

facts.fact: Conceived in 1949, it was one of Denmark's first single-storey schools.
facts.quote: In 1949, Munkegaard School, was conceived as one of the first one-storey schools in Denmark.

facts.fact: The idea was to give a large school the feel of a small one by grouping classrooms in pairs, each with its own courtyard or garden.
facts.quote: The overall idea was to build a complex for a large number of children which had all the advantages of a much smaller school. It was thought this could be achieved by dividing the complex into sets of two adjacent classrooms, each with its own courtyard or garden, in order to provide a feeling of intimacy and wellbeing.

facts.fact: It is a yellow-brick grid of single-storey blocks joined by glass-walled corridors, and each of its 24 classrooms opens onto a courtyard.
facts.quote: The yellow-brick complex consists of a rectangular grid of one-storey buildings linked together by transversal glass-walled corridors. Each of the 24 classrooms has direct access to one of the courtyards between the buildings.

facts.fact: Classrooms get light from full-height windows onto the courtyards and from south-facing clerestories in the split-pitched roofs.
facts.quote: In addition to light from the full-height windows on the walls overlooking the courtyards, daylight comes in through south-facing clerestories in the split-pitched roofs, illuminating the back of the classrooms.

facts.fact: Jacobsen designed nearly everything, from interiors, desks and chairs to lighting, curtains and gardens.
facts.quote: Virtually everything in the school has been designed by Jacobsen: the interiors, fittings, desks and chairs, lighting, curtains, as well as the specially laid out gardens.

facts.fact: Interest in the school led to Jacobsen being chosen to design St Catherine's College, Oxford.
facts.quote: As a result of widespread interest in Munkegård, Jacobsen was chosen to design St Catherine's College, Oxford.

facts.fact: The school was listed in 1996; new facilities were later added beneath the existing buildings under Dorte Mandrup, finished in 2009.
facts.quote: In 1996, Munkegaard School was given the status of a listed building.

facts.fact: The Hôtel Guimard is considered the most important work of Guimard's later period, built in 1909 at 122 avenue Mozart in Paris's 16th arrondissement.
facts.quote: The most important work of this period is the Hôtel Guimard, built in 1909 at 122 avenue Mozart (XVIth arrondissement) in Paris, ten years after his first success with the Hôtel Béranger.

facts.fact: Guimard built it after marrying the American painter Adeline Oppenheim.
facts.quote: It was built following his marriage with Adeline Oppenheim, an American painter from a wealthy family.

facts.fact: The house sits on a triangular plot, and to save space Guimard used an inclined lift instead of a stair on the upper floors.
facts.quote: The house is located on a triangular lot, which proved particularly challenging for Guimard. He saved interior space by installing an inclined elevator rather than a stairway on the upper floors.

facts.fact: The facade shows the house's uses: a part with large windows where his wife painted, and another where he had his office.
facts.quote: The house was designed to show its functions on the façade; his wife could paint in one portion of the house, with large windows, while he worked in his bureau in another part of the house.

facts.fact: Because the plot was too narrow for the outer walls to carry weight, the layout of rooms changes from floor to floor.
facts.quote: Guimard employed some structural innovations, as in the concert hall Humbert-de-Romans (1901), where he created a complex frame to divide sound waves to produce enhanced acoustics (built 1898 and demolished in 1905), or as in the Hôtel Guimard (1909), where the ground was too narrow to have the exterior walls bear any weight, and thus the arrangement of interior spaces differs from one floor to another.

facts.fact: It had a very large dining room but no kitchen, and was meant for working and entertaining.
facts.quote: It had a very large dining room and many tables, but no kitchen; it was apparently designed for working and entertaining.

facts.fact: The house was later split into flats, and its original room layout and furniture are gone.
facts.quote: The house was later broken up into apartments, and the original room arrangements and furniture are gone.

facts.fact: Furniture from the house is now in the Petit Palais, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris and the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon.
facts.quote: Other examples of the late style are from the Hôtel Guimard, now in the Petit Palais and the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris, and Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon.

facts.fact: The Steinhaus at Lake Ossiach is Günther Domenig's own concrete home, which he worked on for more than 30 years.
facts.quote: He is also known for his own concrete home, the Steinhaus at Lake Ossiach, on which he worked for more than 30 years.

facts.fact: The Steinhaus single-family home in Steindorf was built over 1980–2008.
facts.quote: 1980–2008: Single family home Steinhaus, Steindorf

facts.fact: Domenig's first internationally acclaimed work, the Z-bank in Vienna, marked a turn to a more expressionistic, counter-modernist style.
facts.quote: Domenig's first internationally acclaimed completed work was the Z-bank in Vienna, which signalled a much more expressionistic, counter-modernist aesthetic.

facts.fact: The Atheneum is a visitors center in New Harmony, Indiana, by Richard Meier, completed in 1979, and one of the works that first brought him recognition.
facts.quote: Meier first gained recognition for his designs for various houses, for The Atheneum, a visitors center in New Harmony, Indiana (completed 1979), and for the High Museum of Art in Atlanta, Georgia (completed 1983).

facts.fact: The Atheneum is one of New Harmony's contemporary additions, alongside the Roofless Church, in a town of restored Harmonist buildings.
facts.quote: Many of the town's old Harmonist buildings have been restored. These structures, along with others related to the Owenite community, are included in the New Harmony Historic District. Contemporary additions to the town include the Roofless Church and Atheneum.

facts.fact: The Liederhalle is the main concert venue of the Stuttgart Chamber Orchestra.
facts.quote: Its principal concert venue is the Liederhalle, Stuttgart.

facts.fact: Utzon built his own house in Hellebæk, Denmark, in 1952.
facts.quote: Architect's own house, Hellebæk, Denmark, 1952

facts.fact: Having set up his studio in Copenhagen in 1950, Utzon built an open-plan house for himself in 1952, the first of its kind in Denmark.
facts.quote: In 1950 he established his own studio in Copenhagen and, in 1952, built an open-plan house for himself, the first of its kind in Denmark.

facts.fact: The National Building Museum is a museum of architecture, design, engineering, construction and urban planning in Washington, D.C.
facts.quote: The National Building Museum is a museum of architecture, design, engineering, construction, and urban planning in Northwest Washington, D.C., U.S.

facts.fact: It occupies the former Pension Bureau building, a brick building completed in 1887 and designed by Montgomery C. Meigs, the U.S. Army quartermaster general.
facts.quote: The National Building Museum is housed in the former Pension Bureau building, a brick structure completed in 1887 and designed by Montgomery C. Meigs, the U.S. Army quartermaster general.

facts.fact: Meigs broke with the Greco-Roman models used for Washington's government buildings and based his design on Rome's Palazzo Farnese and Palazzo della Cancelleria.
facts.quote: He departed from the established Greco-Roman models that had been the basis of government buildings in Washington, D.C., until then and which continued after the Pension Building's completion. Meigs based his design on Italian Renaissance precedents, notably Rome's Palazzo Farnese and the Palazzo della Cancelleria.

facts.fact: The building centres on a high-columned interior courtyard hall and is an important early large-scale example of Renaissance Revival; it became a National Historic Landmark in 1985.
facts.quote: It is centered around a high-columned interior central courtyard hall often used for various events. It is an important early large-scale example of Renaissance Revival architecture, and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1985.

facts.fact: Caspar Buberl's frieze of Civil War soldiers runs around the outside; 28 scenes were mixed and modified into a continuous 1,200-foot parade of over 1,300 figures.
facts.quote: Because a sculpture of that size was well out of Meigs's budget, he had Buberl create 28 different scenes, totaling 69 feet (21 m) in length, which were then mixed and slightly modified to create the continuous 1,200-foot (365-m) parade of over 1,300 figures.

facts.fact: Built before mechanical ventilation, it was planned for air flow: every office had an outside window and opened onto the court, which drew in cool air at ground level and let hot air out at the roof.
facts.quote: Built before modern artificial ventilation, the building was designed to maximize air circulation: all offices not only had exterior windows, but also opened onto the court, which was designed to admit cool air at ground level and exhaust hot air at the roof.

facts.fact: The interior measures 316 × 116 feet (96 × 35 m) and has been used for inaugural balls.
facts.quote: The vast interior, measuring 316 × 116 feet (96 × 35 m), has been used to hold inauguration balls; a Presidential Seal is set into the floor near the south entrance.

facts.fact: The building, nicknamed "Meigs Old Red Barn", took more than 15 million bricks.
facts.quote: The completed building, sometimes called "Meigs Old Red Barn", required more than 15 million bricks, which, according to the wit of the day, were each counted by the parsimonious Meigs.

facts.fact: The Tribunal de Paris, in the Batignolles district, is France's largest court by caseload.
facts.quote: The Tribunal de Paris (French pronunciation: [tʁibynal d(ə) paʁi], lit. 'Court of Paris'), located at the Judicial Campus of Paris in Batignolles, is the largest court in France by caseload.

facts.fact: Designed by Renzo Piano, the building brings several major and minor courts together under one roof.
facts.quote: Designed by architect Renzo Piano (famous for the Centre Pompidou), the Tribunal de Paris building consolidates several major and minor courts and tribunals into one building.

facts.fact: The building has 38 storeys, stands 160 metres high and has 120,000 square metres of net floor area.
facts.quote: The building is 38 storeys and 160 metres (520 ft) high, and has a total net floor area of 120,000 square metres (1,300,000 ft2).

facts.fact: Inside are 90 courtrooms, 30,000 square metres of offices and 20,000 square metres of public facilities.
facts.quote: Inside the building are 90 law courts, 30,000 square metres (320,000 ft2) of offices and 20,000 square metres (220,000 ft2) of public facilities.

facts.fact: The move from the Palais de Justice was announced in 2009; the building opened in 2018 and was inaugurated in April 2019.
facts.quote: The move from the Palais de Justice was announced on 29 April 2009 by Nicolas Sarkozy, and the contract was signed in 2012. The building was opened in 2018, and was officially inaugurated in April 2019 by French Prime Minister Édouard Philippe.

facts.fact: With the police judicial headquarters and the Paris Bar's offices nearby, it forms the Judicial Campus of Paris.
facts.quote: Located close by is 36, rue du Bastion (Regional Directorate headquarters of the Judicial Paris Police Prefecture) and the Maison de l'ordre des avocats (Offices of the Parisian Bar association) - together, the three buildings form the Judicial Campus of Paris (Cité judiciaire de Paris).

facts.fact: The court used to sit in the Palace of Justice on the Île de la Cité.
facts.quote: The TGI was previously located in the Palace of Justice on the Île de la Cité along with the Court of Appeal of Paris and the Court of Cassation.

facts.fact: The Weltstadthaus is a department store in Cologne designed by Renzo Piano and completed in 2005.
facts.quote: The Weltstadthaus ("global city building"), housing a department store in Cologne, Germany, was designed by Renzo Piano and completed in 2005, following a lengthy legal battle concerning the structural engineering of the core building.

facts.fact: It is built over a main traffic artery, the Nord-Süd-Fahrt, and faces the Schildergasse shopping street.
facts.quote: It covers up a main traffic artery, the Nord-Süd-Fahrt, and faces Europe's most frequented shopping mile, the Schildergasse.

facts.fact: Its organic, ship-like shape earned it the local nickname Walfisch (whale); it is 130 m long and 60 m wide with 14,400 m² of floor space.
facts.quote: With its unusual, organic shape reminiscent of a ship, but also of a stranded whale -- Kölners have dubbed it the Walfisch--it provides 14.400 m² floor space, on a length of 130 m and a width of 60 m.

facts.fact: The 4,900 m² glass facade is made of 6,800 panes carried by 66 laminated beams of Siberian larch.
facts.quote: The 4900 m² glass façade is constructed from 6800 individual panes and 66 massive  laminated beams of Siberian larch.

facts.fact: The atrium looks across five storeys, 36 m high, and the northern facade is clad in 4,400 m² of natural stone.
facts.quote: The atrium offers a view of five stories with a height of 36 m. The 4900 m² glass façade is constructed from 6800 individual panes and 66 massive  laminated beams of Siberian larch. The northern façade consists of 4.400 m² of natural stone.

facts.fact: It has two parts: a stone block that follows the angular 1970s surroundings, and a wood-and-glass shell that flows toward the late Gothic Antoniterkirche.
facts.quote: Wedged between a late Gothic church, the Antoniterkirche, and nondescript post-war concrete, it consists of two distinct parts.  A rectangular block of stone takes up the rhythms of the surrounding seventies' angular forms, while the partially encircling wood-and-glass construction flows toward the church that had looked somewhat displaced previously.

facts.fact: Peek & Cloppenburg commissioned the design, which has won several prizes.
facts.quote: The department store is operated by the German chain Peek & Cloppenburg, which commissioned the Piano design, which has won several prizes.

facts.fact: Behrens built the Eduard Müller Crematorium in Hagen-Delstern between 1905 and 1908.
facts.quote: 1905–1908: Eduard Müller Crematorium in Hagen-Delstern

facts.fact: Behrens's early-1900s work, which included a crematorium, moved toward simple rectilinear volumes and classical sources.
facts.quote: His work in the early 1900s included a series of exhibition halls and pavilions, a crematorium and some private houses, which show a new direction immediately after his own Jugendstil house, towards exploring simple, rectilinear volumes and classical sources.

facts.fact: Pavel Janák's Pardubice Crematorium, the first in the Czech lands, was inspired by Behrens's crematorium in Hagen.
facts.quote: Janák was inspired by Peter Behrens' conception of the crematorium in Hagen.

facts.fact: The Thomas Jefferson Building is the oldest Library of Congress building in Washington, D.C., built between 1890 and 1897.
facts.quote: The Thomas Jefferson Building, also known as the Main Library, is the oldest of the Library of Congress buildings in Washington, D.C. Built between 1890 and 1897, it was initially known as the Library of Congress Building.

facts.fact: It is in the Beaux-Arts and richly decorated Classical Revival styles, known for its classical facade and ornate interior.
facts.quote: The building is designed in the Beaux-Arts and elaborate decorative version of Classical Revival styles of architecture, and is known for its classicizing façade and elaborately decorated interior.

facts.fact: John L. Smithmeyer and Paul J. Pelz won the design competition in 1873, but work was held up by congressional debate until 1886.
facts.quote: John L. Smithmeyer and Paul J. Pelz won the competition for the architectural plans of the library in 1873. The start of the project was delayed by U.S. congressional debates until a vote on the project was held in 1886.

facts.fact: Pelz appears to have been the main designer and oversaw most of the exterior, while Bernard Green and Edward Pearce Casey completed the interiors and their decoration.
facts.quote: While Smithmeyer was instrumental in securing the commission, Pelz appears to have been the main designer of the building and oversaw most of the exterior work. Bernard Green, the superintendent of construction, and Casey are credited for the completion of the interiors and the artistic supervision of the building's unique decorative program.

facts.fact: Its central block is broadly comparable to the Palais Garnier in Paris.
facts.quote: The central block is broadly comparable to the Palais Garnier in Paris, a similarly ambitious expression of triumphant cultural nationalism in the Beaux-Arts style that had triumphed at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, 1893.

facts.fact: The dome over the Main Reading Room, first meant to be under 70 ft tall, was raised to 195 ft and covered in 23-carat gold leaf.
facts.quote: Originally, the dome over the Main Reading Room was intended to be less than 70 ft tall to avoid this critique, however Casey and Green increased the size of the dome to 195 ft and covered it with 23 carat gold leaf.

facts.fact: More than fifty American painters and sculptors made commissioned art for the building.
facts.quote: In total, more than fifty American painters and sculptors produced commissioned works of art.

facts.fact: It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1965.
facts.quote: In 1965, in recognition of the prominent monumental structure and building's historical significance, it was designated a National Historic Landmark (lists maintained by the National Park Service of the United States Department of the Interior).

facts.fact: The Marchiondi Spagliardi Institute in Milan is Vittoriano Viganò's best-known work and is regarded as one of Italy's most significant examples of New Brutalism.
facts.quote: He is best known for the Marchiondi Spagliardi Institute in Milan, regarded as one of the country's most significant examples of New Brutalism.

facts.fact: The institute dates from 1957.
facts.quote: Among his best-known works are the housing for war veterans in the QT8 district (1947, with Ezio Cerutti, Aldo Putelli and Vittorio Gandolfi), the Marchiondi Spagliardi Institute (1957), the Casa "La scala" in Portese, on Lake Garda (1958), the redevelopment plans for Parco Sempione, and the extension of the Faculty of Architecture of the Polytechnic University (1985).

facts.fact: Royan's 1877 neo-Gothic church was destroyed when the town was bombed in January 1945, and a larger, more ambitious church inspired by the great Gothic cathedrals was built after the war.
facts.quote: Royan's 1877 neo-Gothic church, on what is now the Square Charles de Gaulle, was destroyed when Royan was bombed on January 5, 1945. After the war a new church was built, bigger, architecturally ambitious and spectacular, and drawing its aesthetic inspiration from the large Gothic cathedrals.

facts.fact: Notre-Dame de Royan, completed in 1958, is built entirely of reinforced concrete by architects Guillaume Gillet and Marc Hébrard with engineers Bernard Lafaille, René Sarger and Ou Tseng, and is considered a masterpiece of contemporary architecture.
facts.quote: Notre-Dame de Royan, completed in 1958 and built entirely of reinforced concrete by architects Guillaume Gillet and Marc Hébrard and engineers Bernard Lafaille, René Sarger and Ou Tseng, is considered a masterpiece of contemporary architecture.

facts.fact: The elliptical nave is 45 m long and 22 m wide and seats about 2,000 people.
facts.quote: The elliptical nave is 45 metres long by 22 metres wide (148 ft × 72 ft) and has a seating capacity for some 2000 people.

facts.fact: The structure alternates prestressed V-shaped concrete elements, made by engineer Bernard Lafaille's process, with huge windows by Henri Martin-Granel covering 500 square metres.
facts.quote: The building's structure alternates prestressed V-shaped reinforced concrete elements made using the Lafaille process, named for its inventor, French engineer Bernard Lafaille, with huge windows, made by master glazier Henri Martin-Granel and covering a total area of 500 square metres (5,400 sq ft).

facts.fact: The nave is ringed by an ambulatory and a gallery 3 m up, lit by diamond-shaped stained glass showing the Stations of the Cross.
facts.quote: It is flanked by an ambulatory, and a gallery three metres above the floor. The gallery is lit by rhombus-shaped stained glass representing the Stations of the Cross.

facts.fact: The church took three years to build.
facts.quote: The church took three years to build.

facts.fact: It was classified as a historical monument in 1988.
facts.quote: The church was classified as a historical monument in 1988.

facts.fact: The Musiktheater im Revier is Gelsenkirchen's venue for opera, operetta, musical theatre and ballet; it opened on 15 December 1959 and has been a protected monument since 1997.
facts.quote: Musiktheater im Revier (MiR) (Music Theatre in the Ruhr) is the venue for performing opera, operetta, musical theatre and ballet in Gelsenkirchen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It opened on 15 December 1959; it is listed since 1997 as a protected cultural monument.

facts.fact: It has a 1,008-seat Large House and a 336-seat Small House; the auditoria are curved, unlike the cubic exterior.
facts.quote: The building offers two performance spaces: the Large House (Großes Haus) with 1,008 seats and about 200 performances per year, and the Small House (Kleines Haus) with 336 seats and about 120 annual performances. In contrast to the building's outside cubic appearance, the auditoria use a more curved design.

facts.fact: Werner Ruhnau designed it; a 4,500 m² glass facade wraps the Large House and shows the round auditorium casing, the stairs and Yves Klein's two huge sculptures.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the German architect Werner Ruhnau. The cubic outer shell of the Large House is formed by a 4,500 square metres (48,000 sq ft) glass facade, which gives view into the interior and the cylindric casing of the auditorium and its stairways, and the two monumental sculptures by the French artist Yves Klein.

facts.fact: Klein's main relief is a 7 × 20 m blue sponge sculpture in a special "Gelsenkirchen Blue", because International Klein Blue did not work on such large walls.
facts.quote: They consist of one 7×20 m (23×66 ft) monochrome sponge sculpture in a distinctive blue ("Gelsenkirchen Blue") because Klein's International Klein Blue was unsuitable for the large walls: the acetone-based mixture evaporated, the paint lost adhesion and luminescence, and it was highly flammable.

facts.fact: The blue reliefs, seen from outside through the glass, led the city to adopt blue as Gelsenkirchen's house colour.
facts.quote: These intensely blue reliefs, which are visible from the outside through the glass skin of the building, inspired the city's graphic artist, Uwe Gelesch, to introduce blue as Gelsenkirchen's house colour.

facts.fact: The Small House has a mobile by Jean Tinguely.
facts.quote: The Small House features a mobile by Jean Tinguely.

facts.fact: Norbert Kricke's sculpture Röhrendickicht (thicket of pipes, 1957) stands outside the opera house.
facts.quote: One of his more famous works is the Röhrendickicht (thicket of pipes, 1957) outside the Gelsenkirchen opera house Musiktheater im Revier.

facts.fact: The Großmarkthalle was Frankfurt's main wholesale market, mainly for fruit and vegetables; it closed in 2004 and is now part of the European Central Bank's seat.
facts.quote: The Großmarkthalle (Wholesale Market Hall), in Ostend (East End), Frankfurt am Main, was the city's main wholesale market, especially for fruit and vegetables. It closed on 4 June 2004 and the building now forms part of the Seat of the European Central Bank.

facts.fact: It is considered a major example of expressionist architecture.
facts.quote: It is considered a major example of expressionist architecture.

facts.fact: Martin Elsaesser designed it beside Frankfurt's east port as part of the New Frankfurt project, and it opened on 25 October 1928.
facts.quote: The massive structure on the right bank of the Main, immediately adjacent to Frankfurt's east port (Osthafen), was designed by Martin Elsaesser as part of the New Frankfurt-project. It was inaugurated on 25 October 1928.

facts.fact: At 220 m long, 50 m wide and 17–23 m high, it was then the city's largest building.
facts.quote: With a length of 220 m, a width of 50 m and a height of 17 to 23 m (722 by 164 by 55 to 75 ft), it was the city's largest architectural unit at the time.

facts.fact: Its roof spans 50 m freely and was then the world's widest monocoque construction.
facts.quote: The Großmarkthalle Frankfurt am Main is a massively built hall with a roof freely spanning 50 m (164 ft). At the time of its construction it was the world's widest monocoque construction.

facts.fact: The roof is made of 15 concrete barrel vaults (Zeiss-Dywidag shells) only 7 cm thick, engineered by Franz Dischinger and Ulrich Finsterwalder.
facts.quote: The concrete "barrels" (Zeiss-Dywidag barrels) are made of concrete and are only 7 cm (23/4 in) thick. Their basic form is a half ellipse of 6 m (20 ft) height. It was realised between 1926 and 1928 by Franz Dischinger and Ulrich Finsterwalder.

facts.fact: From 1941 the Nazis used the hall as a collecting point for deporting Jews from Frankfurt and the region; a memorial now marks this.
facts.quote: From October 1941 onwards, the Nazis used the Großmarkthalle as a collecting point for the deportation of Jewish men, women and children from Frankfurt and its region.

facts.fact: The preserved main hall now holds the ECB's public spaces, with Coop Himmelb(l)au's twin 180 m towers between it and the river.
facts.quote: The main part of the hall was preserved and mainly houses the public functions of the ECB, such as a visitors' area, the staff restaurant, as well as press and conference spaces. The space between the hall and the Main river is taken up by the Skytower, a complex of two intertwined 180 m (590 ft) skyscrapers, designed by the Vienna-based Coop Himmelb(l)au.

facts.fact: Formerly the Kongresshalle, it was a gift from the United States, designed in 1957 by Hugh Stubbins for the Interbau building exhibition.
facts.quote: It was formerly known as the Kongresshalle conference hall, a gift from the United States, designed in 1957 by the American architect Hugh Stubbins as a part of the Interbau, an International Building Exhibition.

facts.fact: Today it houses Germany's national centre for international contemporary arts, focusing on non-European cultures.
facts.quote: The Haus der Kulturen der Welt (HKW), in English House of World Cultures, in Berlin is Germany's national center for the presentation and discussion of international contemporary arts, with a special focus on non-European cultures and societies.

facts.fact: It stands in the Tiergarten park, next to the Carillon and the German Chancellery.
facts.quote: The Haus der Kulturen der Welt is located in the Tiergarten park, and directly neighbors the Carillon and the new German Chancellery.

facts.fact: The roof collapsed in 1980, killing a journalist; the hall was rebuilt in its original style and reopened in 1987.
facts.quote: On 21 May 1980, the roof collapsed, killing a Sender Freies Berlin radio station journalist and injuring numerous people. The hall was rebuilt in its original style and reopened in 1987 in time for the 750-year anniversary of the founding of Berlin.

facts.fact: Berliners nicknamed it "the pregnant oyster".
facts.quote: Typical of Berlin's popular humor, Berliners have nicknamed the building Die schwangere Auster ("The pregnant Oyster") or "Jimmy Carter's smile".

facts.fact: Henry Moore's heaviest bronze, Large Divided Oval: Butterfly, stands in a pool outside the entrance.
facts.quote: Outside the entrance, Henry Moore's heaviest bronze sculpture, Large Divided Oval: Butterfly (1985–86), stands in the middle of a water basin.

facts.fact: It was one of two high-profile American contributions to Interbau, and Stubbins had once been Walter Gropius's assistant at Harvard.
facts.quote: Interbau featured two high-profile contributions by US architectural firms: The Walter Gropius House by TAC and the Kongresshalle (Convention Centre – today: Haus der Kulturen der Welt) by Hugh Stubbins. Hugh Stubbins formerly worked as Walter Gropius' assistant in 1940 at Harvard University.

facts.fact: Nemausus 1, completed in 1987 in Nîmes, is a housing scheme by Jean Nouvel with 114 apartments.
facts.quote: 1987 – Nemausus 1 (Housing, 114 apartments), Nîmes, France

facts.fact: The Rufer House in Vienna's 13th district was designed by Adolf Loos in 1922 for Josef and Marie Rufer.
facts.quote: The Rufer House at Schließmanngasse 11 in Vienna 13th district, was designed by architect Adolf Loos in 1922 for Josef Rufer and Marie Rufer.

facts.fact: It is considered the first example of Loos's Raumplan (spatial plan), and set the pattern for his later houses.
facts.quote: It is considered to be the first example of Raumplan (literally spatial plan) style. Raumplan differs from its predecessor Free Plan style in its internal spatial organization. While not as well known as other designs by Loos, the Rufer House set the precedent for his later designs.

facts.fact: The house is a cube about 10 × 10 m inside; the outer walls carry the load and the inner walls only divide space.
facts.quote: The house is a cube-like volume with internal dimensions of 10x10 metres. The exterior walls are load-bearing, leaving the interior walls to partition space.

facts.fact: A central column runs through the house, hiding the plumbing and framing views on the second floor.
facts.quote: A central column runs through the house, hiding the plumbing and also acting as a framing device on the second floor.

facts.fact: On the second floor the living area sits lower and the dining room higher, joined by a small stair, so their volumes overlap.
facts.quote: The second floor is made up of the living area on the lower level and the dining room on the higher level.  The dining area is seen as a part of the living area and thus its volumes intersect.

facts.fact: Outside, decoration is kept to a minimum: stark white walls, slim window frames, a cornice and a replica of part of the Parthenon frieze on the street side.
facts.quote: Loos was very adamant about the pure form of the cube above all and decoration is kept to a bare minimum. The walls are a stark white and the window frames contain the least amount of structure. This, however, is balanced by the frieze and cornice that runs along the top of the building, and a replica of some portions of the Parthenon frieze positioned on the street side low enough for viewing.

facts.fact: The windows look random from outside but are placed for light and views from inside.
facts.quote: These interiorly programmed windows give light and views where they make sense on the inside.

facts.fact: The Retti candle shop in Vienna was one of Hollein's early small-scale works, notable for its facade of anodised aluminium.
facts.quote: Hollein's early works were small scale designs, such as the Retti candle shop in Vienna, which notably featured a facade constructed of anodized aluminum.

facts.fact: The shop dates from 1964–65.
facts.quote: 1964–65: Retti candle shop, Vienna, Austria

facts.fact: Hollein founded his own office in Vienna in 1964, after working in Sweden and the United States.
facts.quote: Afterwards, he worked for various architectural firms in Sweden and the United States before returning to Vienna, founding his own office in 1964.

facts.fact: The Hans Otto Theatre is Potsdam's municipal theatre; its main venue is the Großes Haus on the Tiefer See in the Schiffbauergasse cultural district.
facts.quote: The Hans Otto Theatre (German: Hans-Otto-Theater), named after the actor Hans Otto, is a municipal theatre in Potsdam in Germany. Its headquarters and main venue is in the Großes Haus am Tiefen See in Potsdam's cultural district on Schiffbauergasse.

facts.fact: Paul Böhm designed it together with his father Gottfried Böhm: a five-storey theatre with shell-shaped, cantilevered roofs.
facts.quote: The architect Paul Böhm, son of Gottfried Böhm, designed and realised together with his father a five-storey theatre building with shell-shaped, cantilevered roofs.

facts.fact: It is built mainly of concrete, glass and steel, and a listed gas holder was built into the structure.
facts.quote: Concrete, glass and steel are the predominant materials. A listed gas holder was integrated into the structure.

facts.fact: On the lake side it adjoins a listed former chicory mill, now a restaurant.
facts.quote: On the Tiefen See side, a former chicory mill, also a listed building, adjoins the theatre structure; it now houses a restaurant.

facts.fact: The building went up from 2003 to 2006 as a 26.5 million euro project.
facts.quote: The parent building and main venue of the Hans Otto Theatre was built from 2003 to 2006 on the cultural and commercial site Schiffbauergasse (house number 11). The clients of the 26.5 million euro project were the city of Potsdam and the Brandenburg State Development Corporation.

facts.fact: The Großes Haus, opened in 2006, seats 485, and there is an open-air summer stage on the lake.
facts.quote: The main venues on Schiffbauergasse are the Großes Haus, a new stage building opened in 2006 with 485 seats, and the nearby Reithalle with 162 seats. In addition, there is the smaller stage Reithalle Box and the open-air summer stage at the Tiefen See.

facts.fact: It ended a long wait: the theatre had played for fourteen years in a temporary building nicknamed the "tin can" until 2006.
facts.quote: Plays also continued in the "Blechbüchse" – it was the main venue of the Hans Otto Theater GmbH for fourteen years until its final closure in June 2006.

facts.fact: El Capricho is a villa in Comillas, Cantabria, designed by Antoni Gaudí and built in 1883–1885 as a summer house for Máximo Díaz de Quijano.
facts.quote: El Capricho is a villa in Comillas (Cantabria), Spain, designed by Antoni Gaudí. It was built in 1883–1885 for the summer use of a wealthy client, Máximo Díaz de Quijano, who died a year before the house was completed.

facts.fact: It is one of the few buildings Gaudí designed outside Catalonia.
facts.quote: Gaudí, who designed only a small number of buildings outside Catalonia, was involved with other projects at Comillas.

facts.fact: It belongs to Gaudí's early orientalist period, and its tower has been compared to a minaret.
facts.quote: El Capricho belongs to the architect's orientalist period, during the beginnings of Gaudi's artwork. El Capricho allows to see all the foundations on which Modernisme is based, anticipating Europe's avant-garde Art Nouveau. The tower has been compared to a minaret.

facts.fact: The tower is clad in ceramic tiles of yellow sunflowers and green leaves and stands on four classical columns of white stone.
facts.quote: The Tower of El Capricho is covered with beautiful ceramic tiles that alternate between bright yellow sunflowers and green subtle leaves. The top of the minaret tower was done with an arabesque finish. Also notable to mention that at the base of the tower, four classical columns provide support to the heavy tower.

facts.fact: Each of its three floors reads in a different material outside: large stone blocks at the base, small red bricks on the main floor, and a sloping tiled roof above.
facts.quote: The House has 3 floors which are all identifiable by the materials they were built with on the exterior. The basement was built from large stone bricks, the Main floor was made up of smaller red bricks, and the upper floor/ attic area is defined by the beautifully sloped roof and ceramic tiles.

facts.fact: Large windows framed by Gothic-style pointed arches bring daylight inside.
facts.quote: The house also uses many large windows allowing for the use of more natural lighting inside the house. Interestingly, Gaudi uses influence from Gothic Architecture by using pointed arches to frame the windows of the house.

facts.fact: Declared a National Monument in 1969, it was restored as a restaurant in 1988 and became a museum in 2009.
facts.quote: The building fell into disrepair after the Spanish Civil War, a state in which it continued despite being declared a National Monument in 1969. In 1977, the last descendant of the López-Díaz de Quijano family sold the property and it was restored and turned into a restaurant in 1988. Finally, in 2009, the building became a museum.

facts.fact: The Halen Estate is a housing development near Bern, designed and built by Atelier 5 from 1957 to 1961.
facts.quote: The Halen Estate (Siedlung Halen) is a housing development near Berne, Switzerland. It was designed and built by the Atelier 5 architectural partnership from 1957 to 1961.

facts.fact: Set in woodland north of the city, it is an important example of 20th-century Modernist (Structuralist) architecture and is on the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites.
facts.quote: Located in a wooded area north of the city, the development is an important example of 20th century Modernist architecture (Structuralism), and as such is listed on the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites.

facts.fact: It has 82 privately owned houses in three terraces that step down a hillside.
facts.quote: Halen Estate comprises 82 privately owned houses arranged in three terraces. Built on a hillside, the terraces are reminiscent of steps.

facts.fact: The dense estate shares a swimming pool and other communal facilities.
facts.quote: The development, quite dense, is also home to a swimming pool and other communal amenities.

facts.fact: Siedlung Halen became a seminal example of low-rise, high-density housing.
facts.quote: Although the concept of low-rise high-density housing can be traced back to Le Corbusier's unbuilt Roq et Rob project from 1949, a more direct influence was the pioneering work of the Swiss firm Atelier 5, whose Siedlung Halen project built in Bern, Switzerland in 1955-61 became a seminal example of the typology.

facts.fact: It is considered the most influential low-rise, high-density project of the 1960s.
facts.quote: Atelier 5: The Swiss architecture firm designed Siedlung Halen in Bern, Switzerland from 1959-61, which is considered the most influential low-rise, high-density project of the 1960s.

facts.fact: MMM Corones, the sixth and last museum of Reinhold Messner's network, was built on top of Kronplatz (Plan de Corones) at 2,275 m above sea level.
facts.quote: The sixth and last museum of the MMM network, the MMM Corones, was built on the top of the Kronplatz mountain (Plan de Corones in Ladin and Italian) at an altitude of 2,275 meters above sea level.

facts.fact: Designed by Zaha Hadid, it opened in July 2015, with 1,000 square metres of floor space and a permanent exhibition on traditional climbing and mountaineering.
facts.quote: Opened in July 2015, the museum, a modern structure designed by renowned British architect Zaha Hadid, has a floor area of 1,000 square meters and features a permanent exhibition dedicated to traditional climbing and mountaineering.

facts.fact: It is part of the Messner Mountain Museum, created in 2006 by mountaineer Reinhold Messner in South Tyrol.
facts.quote: The Messner Mountain Museum (MMM) is a museum project created in 2006 by Italian mountaineer and extreme climber Reinhold Messner in South Tyrol in northern Italy.

facts.fact: The Villa Jeanneret-Perret, or Maison blanche, was Le Corbusier's first independent project, built in 1912 in his hometown of La Chaux-de-Fonds for his parents.
facts.quote: The Villa Jeanneret-Perret (also known as Maison blanche [mɛzɔ̃ blɑ̃ʃ]) is the first independent project by French-Swiss architect Le Corbusier. Built in 1912 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Charles-Edouard Jeanneret's hometown, it was designed for his parents.

facts.fact: The house sits on the forested hillside above La Chaux-de-Fonds; its horizontal planes contrast with the steep slopes, and its plain white walls stood out from the other houses there.
facts.quote: The Jeanneret-Perret house was larger than the others, and in a more innovative style; the horizontal planes contrasted dramatically with the steep alpine slopes, and the white walls and lack of decoration were in sharp contrast with the other buildings on the hillside.

facts.fact: Its rooms are arranged around four pillars in the central salon, anticipating the open interiors of his later work.
facts.quote: The interior spaces were organized around the four pillars of the salon in the centre, foretelling the open interiors he would create in his later buildings.

facts.fact: Its neo-classical style breaks with local Art Nouveau and draws on his time with Auguste Perret in Paris and Peter Behrens in Berlin.
facts.quote: The Villa Jeanneret-Perret is a witness to the pioneering architecture of the 20th century and the development of Le Corbusier; his characteristic neo-classic style breaks with the regional Art Nouveau and is based on his experience in Paris as a student of Auguste Perret and in Berlin with Peter Behrens.

facts.fact: Jeanneret lived and worked in the house from 1912 to 1915, and it was sold in 1919.
facts.quote: Jeanneret himself lived and worked in the house from 1912 to 1915. In 1919, the house was sold.

facts.fact: The house cost more than he expected, and his parents had to move out within ten years.
facts.quote: The project was more expensive to build than he imagined; his parents were forced to move from the house within ten years and relocate to a more modest house.

facts.fact: Restored by the Association Maison blanche, it has been open to the public since 2005.
facts.quote: It had many owners in the course of the century until 2000, when it was purchased and restored by the "Association Maison blanche" which opened it to the public in 2005.

facts.fact: The Green Building (Building 54) is an academic and research building at MIT that houses the Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences.
facts.quote: The Cecil and Ida Green Building, also called the Green Building or Building 54, is an academic and research building at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The building houses the Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences (EAPS).

facts.fact: It was designed by I. M. Pei, an MIT architecture graduate, with Araldo Cossutta.
facts.quote: The Green Building was designed by I. M. Pei, who received a bachelor's degree in architecture from MIT in 1940, and Araldo Cossutta.

facts.fact: Built in reinforced concrete in 1962–1964, it is 277 feet (84 m) tall, with a concrete facade that echoes the limestone and concrete of older MIT buildings nearby.
facts.quote: The Green Building was constructed during 1962–1964 using reinforced concrete. It has 18 floors, equivalent to 21 stories or 277 feet (84 m) tall, with a concrete facade that resembles the limestone and concrete of the older MIT buildings near it.

facts.fact: From 1964 until 2019 it was the tallest building in Cambridge.
facts.quote: From its completion in 1964, the Green Building was the tallest building in Cambridge, until it was surpassed in 2019 by Site 4 in nearby Kendall Square.

facts.fact: To get around a city limit on the number of floors, it was raised on stilts, with the first occupied floor about 30 feet above the ground.
facts.quote: When it was built, Cambridge law limited the number of floors for high-rise buildings. Thus, the Green Building was designed to be on stilts, with the first occupied floor approximately 30 feet (9.1 m) above ground level, in order to "circumvent" this law and maximize the building's height.

facts.fact: Its height serves a purpose: the roof carries weather instruments, radio equipment and a white radome around a weather radar.
facts.quote: The building's height has some functional purpose. Its roof supports meteorological instruments and radio communications equipment, plus a white spherical radome enclosing long-distance weather radar apparatus.

facts.fact: Strong winds in the archway at its base sometimes stopped people using the doors; a 2019 renovation filled in the archway with a larger entry pavilion.
facts.quote: A 2019 renovation and expansion project completely filled the problematic open archway, incorporating the cavity into an expanded entry pavilion.

facts.fact: Its grid of large windows has been used by MIT students as a giant display, including a playable Tetris game in 2012.
facts.quote: On April 20, 2012, MIT hackers successfully turned the Green Building into a huge, playable Tetris game, operated from a wireless control podium at a comfortable viewing distance in front of the building.

facts.fact: The Gateway is a pair of 37-storey, 150 m office towers on Beach Road in Singapore's Downtown Core, completed in April 1990.
facts.quote: The Gateway is a 37-storey, 150 m (490 ft), skyscraper complex completed in April 1990 on Beach Road in the Downtown Core of Singapore. The two buildings are named The Gateway East and The Gateway West.

facts.fact: The towers were designed by I. M. Pei, with the local firm Chua Ka Seng and Partners and structural engineers T.Y. Lin.
facts.quote: The buildings were designed by the U.S.-based architect, I. M. Pei. The local Singaporean architectural firm that worked on this project was Chua Ka Seng and Partners Chartered Architects (CKSP).  T.Y. Lin Structural Engineers from San Francisco also collaborated on the project.

facts.fact: The buildings are trapezoidal in plan, a form Pei also used for the National Gallery of Art East Building in Washington, D.C.
facts.quote: The shape of the buildings is trapezoidal, which is similar to the form used by I. M. Pei in the critically acclaimed National Gallery of Art East Building in Washington, D.C.

facts.fact: Singapore's National Library Board has described its architecture as "world class".
facts.quote: The architecture of The Gateway has been described as "world class" by the National Library Board.

facts.fact: Society Hill Towers is a complex of three 31-storey residential towers with 624 units on a 5-acre site in Philadelphia's Society Hill.
facts.quote: The Society Hill Towers are a three-building condominium complex located in the Society Hill neighborhood of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The complex contains three 31-story skyscrapers with 624 units on a 5-acre (2.0 ha) site.

facts.fact: Designed by I. M. Pei and Associates, the towers are built of cast-in-place concrete and every apartment has floor-to-ceiling windows.
facts.quote: The towers were designed by I. M. Pei and Associates and are constructed of cast-in-place concrete, with each apartment featuring floor-to-ceiling windows.

facts.fact: Completed in 1964 as rental flats, they became condominiums in 1979.
facts.quote: Completed in 1964, the apartments were originally rental units but were converted to condominiums in 1979.

facts.fact: They were part of the redevelopment of Society Hill, then considered a slum, on land cleared of the Dock Street Market.
facts.quote: In the late 1950s, Society Hill was considered a slum neighborhood, which was targeted for redevelopment by the Philadelphia City Planning Commission and the Redevelopment Authority.

facts.fact: Pei paired the three towers with low-rise Society Hill Townhouses.
facts.quote: Architect I. M. Pei and his team created a plan for three 31-story Society Hill Towers as well as the Society Hill Townhouses, a low-rise project.

facts.fact: The towers brought a cubist design into an 18th-century neighbourhood, with green space and traditional townhouses easing the transition.
facts.quote: Pei designed the Society Hill Towers, a three-building residential block injecting cubist design into the local 18th-century milieu. As with previous projects, abundant green spaces were central to Pei's vision, which added traditional townhouses to aid the transition from classical to modern design.

facts.fact: The buildings were added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1999.
facts.quote: The buildings were listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places on March 10, 1999.

facts.fact: Harvard's Smith Campus Center, formerly Holyoke Center, is a brutalist administrative and service building in Harvard Square, opposite the Wadsworth Gate to Harvard Yard.
facts.quote: Harvard University's Smith Campus Center (formerly Holyoke Center) is a brutalist administrative and service building located in Harvard Square, Cambridge, Massachusetts. Opposite the Wadsworth Gate to Harvard Yard on Massachusetts Avenue, it functions as a student center, as well as housing Harvard administrative offices, University Health Services, and a restaurant arcade.

facts.fact: Designed mainly by Josep Lluís Sert, then dean of Harvard's Graduate School of Design, and completed in 1966, it is an H-shaped, ten-storey reinforced concrete building.
facts.quote: Primarily designed by Josep Lluís Sert (then dean of the Harvard Graduate School of Design) and completed in 1966, the Smith Campus Center is an H-shaped ten-story reinforced concrete building.

facts.fact: It was built in two phases between 1960 and 1966.
facts.quote: The building was constructed in two phases over a six-year period between 1960 and 1966.

facts.fact: It was Harvard's first high-rise, nicknamed a "gray elephant" for its concrete facades.
facts.quote: It was Harvard's first highrise building, and has been called a "gray elephant" for the color of its concrete facades.

facts.fact: Within a few years its exterior concrete began crumbling and its three-pipe heating and cooling system proved inefficient.
facts.quote: These included crumbling of exterior structural concrete and an inefficient three-pipe heating and cooling system.

facts.fact: From 1964 to 1979 its penthouse dining room held five large paintings by Mark Rothko, removed after sunlight faded them badly.
facts.quote: From 1964 to 1979, the penthouse dining room was decorated with five large paintings installed by Mark Rothko, an Abstract Expressionist artist.

facts.fact: Originally Holyoke Center, it was renamed the Richard A. and Susan F. Smith Campus Center in 2013.
facts.quote: Originally known as Holyoke Center, in 2013 it was renamed the Richard A. and Susan F. Smith Campus Center.

facts.fact: After years of renovation into gathering, study, exhibition and event spaces, it reopened in 2018.
facts.quote: Over the next several years, its underwent extensive renovation to create gathering, lounge, and study spaces, and space for exhibitions, events, and performances, after reopening in 2018.

facts.fact: The Palmolive Building is a 37-storey Art Deco building at 919 N. Michigan Avenue in Chicago.
facts.quote: The Palmolive Building, formerly the Playboy Building, is a 37-story Art Deco building at 919 N. Michigan Avenue in Chicago, Illinois.

facts.fact: Designed by Holabird & Root, it was completed in 1929 as the headquarters of the Colgate-Palmolive-Peet Company.
facts.quote: Designed by Holabird & Root, the Palmolive Building was completed in 1929 as the home of the Colgate-Palmolive-Peet Company.

facts.fact: From 1965 it was the Playboy Building, home of Playboy magazine's offices until 1989.
facts.quote: Playboy Enterprises purchased the leasehold in 1965 and the structure was renamed the Playboy Building.  It was home to the editorial and business offices of Playboy magazine until 1989, when Playboy moved its offices to 680 N Lake Shore Drive.

facts.fact: It became a Chicago Landmark in 2000 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2003.
facts.quote: The building was designated a Chicago Landmark in 2000, and it was added to the federal National Register of Historic Places in 2003.

facts.fact: After 2001 it was converted to housing with Booth Hansen Architects, keeping offices and shops on the first two floors.
facts.quote: In 2001, the building was sold to developer Draper and Kramer who, with Booth Hansen Architects, converted it to residential use, with the first two floors dedicated to upscale office and retail space.

facts.fact: In 1930 a rotating beacon named after Charles Lindbergh was added on top to help guide planes to Midway Airport.
facts.quote: A beacon named for the aviator Charles Lindbergh was added to the building in 1930. It rotated a full 360 degrees and was intended to help guide airplanes safely to Midway Airport.

facts.fact: Villa Fallet is a chalet in La Chaux-de-Fonds designed and built by the eighteen-year-old Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, later known as Le Corbusier.
facts.quote: Villa Fallet is a traditional chalet located in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland designed and built by the eighteen-year-old Charles-Édouard Jeanneret (1887–1965), who later became better known as Le Corbusier.

facts.fact: It was his first house, designed with two other students under their teacher René Chapallaz for the engraver Louis Fallet.
facts.quote: In 1905, he and two other students, under the supervision of their teacher, René Chapallaz, designed and built his first house, the Villa Fallet, for the engraver Louis Fallet, a friend of another of his teachers, Charles l'Eplattenier.

facts.fact: The house is in the Style Sapin, the Swiss variant of Art Nouveau.
facts.quote: The house is in the Style Sapin, the Swiss variant of Art Nouveau.

facts.fact: It is a large chalet with a steep roof in the local alpine style, its facade decorated with coloured geometric patterns of triangular pine trees and pine cones.
facts.quote: The chalet on the forested hillside near La Chaux-de-Fonds, is a large traditional chalet with a steep roof in the local alpine style, and is decorated with carefully crafted colored geometric patterns on the façade, with a design of triangular pine trees and pine cones.

facts.fact: Its success led to two similar houses nearby, the Villas Jacquemet and Stotzer.
facts.quote: The success of this house led to his construction of two similar houses, the Villas Jacquemet and Stotzer, in the same area.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1905 and is recognised as a building of cultural significance in Switzerland.
facts.quote: It was completed in 1905. It is now recognised as a building of cultural significance in Switzerland.

facts.fact: Chapallaz, Jeanneret's architecture teacher, strongly influenced his earliest houses.
facts.quote: His architecture teacher was architect René Chapallaz, who had a large influence on Le Corbusier's earliest house designs.

facts.fact: The Großes Festspielhaus is an opera house in Salzburg designed by Clemens Holzmeister in 1956 to host the Salzburg Festival.
facts.quote: The Großes Festspielhaus (Large Festival House), is an Austrian opera theatre house, that in its current form, was designed by architect Clemens Holzmeister in 1956 to host the Salzburg Festival..

facts.fact: It opened on 26 July 1960 with Der Rosenkavalier conducted by Herbert von Karajan, who also worked with Holzmeister on parts of the design.
facts.quote: It was inaugurated on 26 July 1960 with a performance of Richard Strauss' Der Rosenkavalier conducted by Herbert von Karajan, who also worked with Holzmeister on aspects of the building's design.

facts.fact: The building tunnels into the Mönchsberg and has a 2,179-seat hall that can be scaled down acoustically for recitals.
facts.quote: The Large Festival House includes office space and tunneling into the Mönchsberg as well as a 2,179-seat performance space adaptable for both scenic and non-scenic events and acoustically scalable down for piano and song recitals.

facts.fact: Its stage, 100 m wide, is one of the widest in the world.
facts.quote: The stage is one of the widest in the world, at 100 metres (330 ft).

facts.fact: The auditorium is square, and five bronze doors lead from the street into the lobby beneath a Latin inscription.
facts.quote: The auditorium is square. Access from the street to the lobby is through five bronze doors, above which is inscribed a Latin motto by Thomas Michels: SACRA CAMENAE DOMUS / CONCITIS CARMINE PATET / QUO NOS ATTONITOS / NUMEN AD AURAS FERAT (The Muse's holy house is open to those moved by song / divine power may bear us up who are inspired).

facts.fact: Holzmeister designed it after returning to Austria in 1954 from years of work in Turkey.
facts.quote: He remained in Turkey until 1954, then returned to Austria, where his 1950s commissions include the Großes Festspielhaus.

facts.fact: It was built from 1955 to 1960.
facts.quote: Grosses Festspielhaus in Salzburg (1955-1960)

facts.fact: The Richard B. Fisher Center is the performance hall of Bard College in Annandale-on-Hudson, New York, for music, theatre, dance and opera.
facts.quote: The Richard B. Fisher Center for the Performing Arts at Bard College is a performance hall located in the Hudson Valley hamlet of Annandale-on-Hudson, New York. The center provides audiences with performances and programs in orchestral, chamber, and jazz music, and in theater, dance, and opera.

facts.fact: Designed by Frank Gehry, the 110,000-square-foot centre holds two theatres and four rehearsal studios.
facts.quote: Designed by architect Frank Gehry, the 110,000-square-foot (10,000 m2) center houses two theaters, four rehearsal studios for dance, theater, and music, and professional support facilities.

facts.fact: Its heating and air conditioning run entirely on geothermal energy, so it uses no fossil fuel in normal operation.
facts.quote: The building's heat and air-conditing systems are entirely powered by geothermal sources, enabling the Fisher Center to be fossil fuel free during standard operations.

facts.fact: It cost 2 million, took three years to build and opened in April 2003.
facts.quote: The total cost of the project reached $62 million and took three years to complete, opening in April 2003.

facts.fact: The New Yorker called it possibly the best small concert hall in the United States.
facts.quote: The New Yorker calls it "[possibly] the best small concert hall in the United States."

facts.fact: The 900-seat Sosnoff Theater has acoustics by Yasuhisa Toyota, with an acoustic shell that turns it into a concert hall.
facts.quote: The Sosnoff Theater, an intimate, 900-seat theater with an orchestra, parterre, and two balcony sections, features an orchestra pit for opera and acoustics designed by Yasuhisa Toyota, including an acoustic shell that turns the theater into a concert hall for performances of chamber and symphonic music.

facts.fact: The smaller LUMA Theater is a flexible 200-seat space for Bard's theatre and dance programmes.
facts.quote: The smaller of the two theaters is the flexible 200-seat LUMA Theater, which houses Bard's Theater and Dance Programs during the academic year.

facts.fact: Westmount Square is a residential and office complex in Westmount, Quebec, with two apartment buildings and two office buildings.
facts.quote: Westmount Square (French: Carré Westmount) is a residential and office complex located in Westmount, Quebec, Canada. There are two residential apartment buildings and two office buildings.

facts.fact: The towers stand on an underground shopping centre, linked by tunnel to Place Alexis Nihon, Dawson College and Atwater Metro station.
facts.quote: These towers sit atop an underground shopping centre consisting of thirty-five shops. It is located between Sainte Catherine Street West and De Maisonneuve Boulevard West and between Wood Avenue and Greene Avenue. It is connected to Place Alexis Nihon, Dawson College, and the Atwater Metro station by a tunnel.

facts.fact: Mies van der Rohe designed it in the International Style; construction began in 1964 and it opened on 13 December 1967.
facts.quote: The complex was designed by architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe in the International Style. Construction began in 1964 and the complex opened on 13 December 1967.

facts.fact: Its curtain walls are black anodised aluminium with smoked glass, modelled on his Lake Shore Drive Apartments in Chicago.
facts.quote: The exterior facade features curtain walls, and is made of black anodized aluminium and smoked glass windows. It was modelled on Lake Shore Drive Apartments in Chicago.

facts.fact: The main office tower has 22 floors and is 83 m tall; the two residential towers have 21 floors each and are 69 m tall.
facts.quote: The office building, also known as Tower 1, has 22 floors and stands 83 metres (272 ft) tall. The other office building has 2 floors and is known as the Tower 4 Pavilion; it was formerly the Eastern Airlines Building. The two residential towers each have 21 floors, and stand 69 metres (226 ft) tall.

facts.fact: Skylights added to the shopping concourse roof in 1990 were criticised by preservationists.
facts.quote: Skylights were installed on the roof of the shopping concourse in 1990, which led to criticism among architectural preservationists.

facts.fact: The Pantheon is a cenotaph in Brasília honouring national heroes, conceived after the 1985 death of president-elect Tancredo Neves.
facts.quote: The Tancredo Neves Pantheon of the Fatherland and Freedom (Portuguese: Panteão da Pátria e da Liberdade Tancredo Neves) is a cenotaph in the Brazilian capital Brasília, dedicated to the honour of national heroes. It was conceived during the national shock following the death in 1985 of president-elect Tancredo Neves, the first elected civilian president after twenty years of military rule.

facts.fact: Unlike other national pantheons, it holds no tombs.
facts.quote: Unlike other national pantheons it is not a mausoleum and does not contain any tombs.

facts.fact: It stands in the Praça dos Três Poderes and was designed by Oscar Niemeyer as a modernist building symbolising a dove.
facts.quote: It is located in the Praça dos Três Poderes in Brasilia. It was designed by Oscar Niemeyer as a modernist building symbolizing a dove.

facts.fact: François Mitterrand laid its foundation stone in October 1985, and it opened on 7 September 1986.
facts.quote: Its foundation stone was laid by French President François Mitterrand on 15 October 1985 and the Pantheon was inaugurated on 7 September 1986.

facts.fact: It has three floors with 2,105 m² in all; the Red Hall holds Athos Bulcão's Mural of Freedom.
facts.quote: The Pantheon has three floors with a total area of 2,105 m2 (22,660 sq ft). Inside in the Red Hall is the Mural of Freedom by Athos Bulcão.

facts.fact: The third floor has stained glass by Marianne Peretti, who also made the glass for Brasília's cathedral.
facts.quote: On the third floor is stained glass by Marianne Peretti, who also designed the glass for the Cathedral of Our Lady Aparecida in Brasilia.

facts.fact: An eternal flame for freedom and independence burns on top of a diagonal tower outside.
facts.quote: On the outside, on top of a tower built on the diagonal, burns an eternal flame which represents the freedom of the people and the country's independence.

facts.fact: It was listed by Brazil's national heritage institute in 2007 with 34 other Niemeyer works.
facts.quote: The Pantheon was listed in 2007 by the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage along with 34 other works of the then 100-year-old Oscar Niemeyer.

facts.fact: Villa Esche in Chemnitz is an Art Nouveau villa designed and built by Henry van de Velde in 1902/1903 and extended in 1911.
facts.quote: The Villa Esche in the Chemnitz locality of Helbersdorf in Saxony, Germany, is an Art Nouveau villa designed and built by the Belgian architect and designer Henry van de Velde (1863–1957) in 1902/1903 and extended in 1911.

facts.fact: Built for textile manufacturer Herbert Esche, it is considered van de Velde's first commission in Germany and the start of modern architecture in Chemnitz.
facts.quote: The house for the textile entrepreneur Herbert Esche (1874–1962) and his family is considered van de Velde's first commission in Germany, and thus also the begin of modern architecture in Chemnitz.

facts.fact: The villa is a Gesamtkunstwerk: furniture, textiles and everyday objects, down to clothing, were part of the design.
facts.quote: The villa is a Gesamtkunstwerk (total artwork) in the sense of Art Nouveau. Furniture, interior textiles, and everyday objects, all the way down to clothing, are part of it.

facts.fact: Its small surrounding park was probably designed by van de Velde's wife, Maria Séthe.
facts.quote: The small park surrounding the villa was probably designed by van de Velde's wife Maria Séthe.

facts.fact: After serving the Soviet military, the Stasi and a school, and standing empty from 1989, it was renovated between 1998 and 2001.
facts.quote: The villa was the seat of the Chemnitz Soviet military commander in 1945, served as a residence from 1947, was used by the Ministry for State Security from 1952, was an educational institution from 1964 and stood empty from 1989. It was renovated and rebuilt between 1998 and 2001 by the architect Werner Wendisch and partly with the architect Karl-Heinz Barth.

facts.fact: It now houses a Henry van de Velde Museum, part of the Chemnitz Art Collections, showing original furnishings.
facts.quote: Today, the building houses a Henry van de Velde Museum (concept: Klaus-Jürgen Sembach) as part of the Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz (Chemnitz Art Collections); here, mainly parts of the original furnishings of the house, also designed by van de Velde, are presented.

facts.fact: Villa Esche and Villa Leuring show van de Velde's Art Nouveau style in architecture.
facts.quote: Around the turn of the century, he designed Villa Leuring in the Netherlands, and Villa Esche in Chemnitz, two works that show his Art Nouveau style in architecture.

facts.fact: The Perret Tower in Grenoble (1925) was the first concrete tower, built for the International Exhibition of Hydropower and Tourism to demonstrate Perret's "Order of Concrete".
facts.quote: He also created innovative industrial buildings, including a warehouse in Casablanca covered with a think veil of concrete (1915); the Perret Tower, the first concrete tower for the International Exhibition of Hydropower and Tourism of Grenoble (1925), to demonstrate his "Order of Concrete"; and the church of Notre Dame du Raincy (1922–23), where the interior columns were left undecorated and the concrete vaults of the ceiling became the most prominent decorative feature.

facts.fact: France declared the Perret Tower in Grenoble a national heritage site in 1998.
facts.quote: In 1998, the Perret Tower in Grenoble was declared a national heritage site by France.

facts.fact: In his later works Perret used concrete imaginatively while keeping classical harmony, symmetry and proportion.
facts.quote: In his later works, Perret used concrete in imaginative ways to achieve the functions of his buildings, while preserving classical harmony, symmetry and proportions.

facts.fact: The Glaspalast Sindelfingen was designed by Behnisch & Partner in 1976 and was refurbished and technically upgraded by Behnisch Architekten in 2015.
facts.quote: 2015 Glaspalast Sindelfingen (designed by Behnisch & Partner 1976) – Refurbishment and Technical Upgrade, Sindelfingen, Germany

facts.fact: Muziekcentrum Vredenburg was a music venue in Utrecht for 5,000 people, designed by Herman Hertzberger.
facts.quote: Muziekcentrum Vredenburg was a music venue in Utrecht, Netherlands with a capacity of 5,000 people. It was designed by Dutch architect Herman Hertzberger.

facts.fact: Apart from its main hall, the building was demolished and replaced by a larger venue on the same site.
facts.quote: The old building (except the main hall) has been demolished and the city of Utrecht has built a new, bigger venue on the same location.

facts.fact: The old main hall is now part of TivoliVredenburg, which opened in July 2014.
facts.quote: The main hall of the old building has been integrated into the new building. The new building was officially opened in July 2014 and is called TivoliVredenburg.

facts.fact: Most of the building was demolished in 2008.
facts.quote: Muziekcentrum Vredenburg, a music venue in Utrecht, designed by Herman Hertzberger; mostly demolished in 2008

facts.fact: The Skagen Odde Nature Centre, near the northern tip of the peninsula, is a museum built to help visitors see, hear and understand the area's sand, water, wind and light.
facts.quote: The Skagen Odde Nature Centre located close to the northern tip of the peninsula is a museum specially built to allow visitors to see, hear and understand more about the area's sand, water, wind and light.

facts.fact: Each of its pavilions presents one of these elements in its own atmosphere.
facts.quote: Each of the pavilions presents one of these elements in a special atmosphere.

facts.fact: Designed by Jørn Utzon, it is the most northerly building on Skagen Odde.
facts.quote: Designed by Jørn Utzon, it is the most northerly building on Skagen Odde.

facts.fact: Utzon designed it in 1989; his son Jan Utzon completed it in 1999–2000.
facts.quote: Skagen Odde Nature Centre, Skagen, Denmark, 1989 (completed by his son Jan Utzon in 1999–2000)

facts.fact: Utzon's work grew from a Nordic concern for nature, which he developed into what he called Additive Architecture, likened to the growth patterns of nature.
facts.quote: Utzon had a Nordic sense of concern for nature which, in his design, emphasized the synthesis of form, material and function for social values. His fascination with the architectural legacies of the ancient Mayas, the Islamic world, China, and Japan also informed his practice. This developed into what Utzon later referred to as Additive Architecture, comparing his approach to the growth patterns of nature.

facts.fact: The Marine Traffic Control Tower for the Port of Lisbon Authority is one of Gonçalo Byrne's most relevant works.
facts.quote: Included in his diversified body of work, in terms of scale, theme and programme, the more relevant examples are the recent interventions in the Monastery of Alcobaça and its surrounding areas, the building for the Headquarters of the Government of the Province of Flemish Brabant in Leuven, Belgium, the Marine Traffic Control Tower for the Port of Lisbon Authority, the "Império" Quarter in the Chiado area of Lisbon, the Faro Theatre in the Algarve, and the National Museum Machado de Castro, in Coimbra, this latter project currently under construction.

facts.fact: The VTS Tower in Lisbon is a centre for coordinating and controlling maritime traffic, listed under 1997 in Byrne's works.
facts.quote: 1997 - VTS Tower - Maritime traffic coordination and control centre, Lisbon

facts.fact: The Gosstrakh apartments on Malaya Bronnaya Street in Moscow were designed by Moisei Ginzburg in 1926.
facts.quote: The earliest of these projects was the Gosstrakh apartments on Malaya Bronnaya Street in Moscow, designed in 1926.

facts.fact: These flats were the first use in the USSR of Le Corbusier's 'Five Points of Modern Architecture'.
facts.quote: These flats represented the first application in the USSR of Le Corbusier's 'Five Points of Modern Architecture'.

facts.fact: The writer Sergei Tretyakov rented one of the apartments.
facts.quote: One of the apartments was rented by Sergei Tretyakov.

facts.fact: They are among the built collective housing projects of the Constructivist movement, alongside Ginzburg's more famous Narkomfin Building.
facts.quote: Collective housing projects that were built included Ivan Nikolaev's Communal House of the Textile Institute (Ordzhonikidze St, Moscow, 1929–1931), and Ginzburg's Moscow Gosstrakh apartments and, most famously, his Narkomfin Building.

facts.fact: Ginzburg's 1924 book Style and Epoch served as a manifesto for Constructivist architecture.
facts.quote: In 1924, he published Style and Epoch, an influential work of architectural theory that has often been compared to Le Corbusier's Vers une architecture. The book functioned as a manifesto for Constructivist Architecture, a movement that combined advanced technology and engineering principles with socialist ideology.

facts.fact: Housing, especially collective housing, was the main priority of the OSA Group that Ginzburg co-founded in 1925.
facts.quote: In 1925 the OSA Group, also with ties to Vkhutemas, was founded by Alexander Vesnin and Moisei Ginzburg—the Organisation of Contemporary Architects. This group had much in common with Weimar Germany's Functionalism, such as the housing projects of Ernst May. Housing, especially collective housing in specially designed dom kommuny to replace the collectivised 19th century housing that was the norm, was the main priority of this group.

facts.fact: Langer Eugen is an office tower in Bonn's Gronau district, built between 1966 and 1969, which until 1999 held the offices of the members of the Bundestag.
facts.quote: Langer Eugen (English: "Tall Eugene") is an office tower in the Gronau district of Bonn, Germany.  It was built between 1966 and 1969.  Since 2006 it has housed several United Nations organizations.  Until the German Bundestag (parliament) moved to Berlin in 1999, the building was the primary location for the offices of the members of the Bundestag.

facts.fact: Egon Eiermann, one of Germany's most prominent architects of the time, received the design contract in March 1965.
facts.quote: In March 1965, Egon Eiermann, one of the most prominent German architects of the period, received the contract for the design and the artistic management.

facts.fact: The tower is 115 m high with 30 storeys and three basement levels.
facts.quote: According to the specifications, the building is 115 meters high, distributed over 30 stories, with an additional three basement levels.

facts.fact: Its frame is entirely steel, unusual in central Europe, making it Germany's tallest steel-framed building.
facts.quote: The frame of the building is made entirely of steel.  This is highly unusual in central European construction where most buildings use concrete frames.  Therefore, even though it is only the 43rd tallest building in Germany, it is actually the tallest building in Germany with a steel frame.

facts.fact: It was listed less than 30 years after completion; its facade without hierarchy was seen as a vivid example of democratic building in young West Germany.
facts.quote: Preservationists justified their decision, stating that the building, with its eschewal of hierarchical elements in the facade design, was a "vivid example for the understanding of democratic construction in the young West Germany."

facts.fact: Its name, "Tall Eugene", jokes about the short Bundestag President Eugen Gerstenmaier, who drove its construction.
facts.quote: The building's name, "Langer Eugen" ("Tall Eugene") is an ironic reference to the short stature of Eugen Gerstenmaier (the implied "Short Eugene"), who was President of the Bundestag when the tower was built, and was the driving force behind its construction.

facts.fact: When it was renovated for the United Nations, few substantial changes were made, to preserve Eiermann's architecture.
facts.quote: The renovations made few substantial alterations in order to preserve Eiermann's architecture as much as possible.

facts.fact: When built, it was briefly the second-tallest building in Germany.
facts.quote: When it was built it was briefly the second-tallest building in Germany, behind the Bayer-Hochhaus.

facts.fact: PPG Place is a complex of six buildings over three city blocks and five and a half acres in downtown Pittsburgh, designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee.
facts.quote: PPG Place is a complex in downtown Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, consisting of six buildings within three city blocks and five and a half acres. PPG Place was designed by architects Philip Johnson and John Burgee.
